learning_outcomes.text: Manipulate and operate real functions of a real variable, obtaining limits, derivatives, and primitive functions.
Know and apply the properties and techniques of differential and integral calculus, in one and several variables, to solve problems similar to those posed in the field of engineering.
Acquire agility in the calculation and manipulation of mathematical expressions.
Identify a mathematical problem, apply the necessary techniques to solve it, and evaluate the obtained results.
Model problems similar to those posed in engineering using mathematical tools and proceed to solve them.
Understand and rigorously use mathematical language.
Is capable of abstract reasoning, with logical and algorithmic thinking.
Is capable of working in a team, applying critical reasoning, making decisions, and communicating knowledge and conclusions in the field of industrial engineering.

syllabus_topics: Differentiation of functions of one and several variables
Integration of functions of one variable
Cartesian, polar, elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic coordinate systems
Parameterization of curves and surfaces in different coordinate systems
Unit 2: Real functions of a real variable
Critical points: relative extrema. Absolute extrema. Optimization
Taylor polynomial in one variable. Lagrange remainder and upper bound for absolute error
Unit 3: Real functions of several real variables
Directional derivative. Partial derivatives and gradient vector
Critical points: relative extrema. Absolute extrema. Conditioned extrema: optimization and Lagrange multipliers. Saddle points
Unit 5: Integration in a real variable
Calculation of primitives: immediate, by parts, change of variable, rational, trigonometric, and irrational
Riemann integral and fundamental theorem of calculus
Line integration: circulation of a vector field
Double and triple integration and Fubini's theorem
Surface integration: flux of a vector field
assessment_rules: For ordinary call continuous assessment, the final grade is the weighted average of four exercise submissions (7.5% each) and four individual exams (17.5% each); a final grade of 5.0 or higher passes the course. If continuous assessment is not passed, students can take a single exam in June, divided into two parts (50% each for the first and second semester). In this case, students can choose to retake only the failed semester or the entire course, needing 5.0 or higher to pass. For the extraordinary call in July, a single exam covers all course content, or only the failed semester if one was passed in the ordinary call, with the final grade being the arithmetic mean of the two semester grades (50% each) and requiring 5.0 or higher to pass. Grades are on a scale of 0-10: 0-4.9 (Fail), 5.0-6.9 (Pass), 7.0-8.9 (Good), 9.0-10 (Excellent).
